q: All Indian stock and index options are:
e: All Indian exchange-traded equity and index options are European — exercisable only on the expiry date. American-style options are not traded on Indian exchanges.

q: A call option is in-the-money when:
o: Spot price is greater than strike price
Spot price is lower than strike price
Premium is greater than strike price
e: Call ITM = Spot > Strike (the holder has the right to buy below the market). Put ITM is the mirror: Spot < Strike.

q: Intrinsic value of an option:
o: Can be negative if option is OTM
Is the option premium minus the strike
e: Intrinsic value is max(S − X, 0) for a call and max(X − S, 0) for a put — never negative. The holder simply wouldn't exercise if it would result in a loss.

q: The premium of an at-the-money option consists entirely of:
e: ATM and OTM options have zero intrinsic value; their premium is entirely time value. Time value decays toward zero as expiry approaches.

q: Which Greek measures the rate of change of an option's price with respect to time?
e: Theta = sensitivity to time decay. It is negative for long options (buyer loses value daily) and positive for short options (writer earns value daily).

q: Vega measures sensitivity of an option's price to:
e: Vega measures sensitivity to changes in implied volatility. Higher IV raises premium for both calls and puts (vega is positive for any long option).

q: The break-even point at expiry for a long call (Strike X, Premium P) is:
e: Long call BEP = Strike + Premium. The buyer needs the spot to rise above (X + P) at expiry to recover the premium and start profiting.

q: The break-even point at expiry for a long put (Strike X, Premium P) is:
e: Long put BEP = Strike − Premium. The buyer profits when spot falls below (X − P).

q: An option writer (seller) of a naked call faces:
e: Naked call writer's max gain = premium received (limited). Loss is theoretically unlimited because the underlying can rise without bound.

q: Delta of a deep in-the-money call option approaches:
e: Deep ITM call delta approaches +1 (behaves almost like the underlying). ATM call delta ≈ 0.5; deep OTM call delta approaches 0.

q: If Nifty spot is 24,000, the strike price 24,100 call option is best described as:
e: Spot 24,000 < Strike 24,100 → call is OTM. The right to buy at 24,100 has no immediate payoff when the underlying is at 24,000.

q: A call option's premium is ₹50 with strike ₹100; spot is ₹120. The intrinsic value is:
e: Call intrinsic = max(S − X, 0) = max(120 − 100, 0) = ₹20. Time value = Premium − Intrinsic = 50 − 20 = ₹30.

q: Put-call parity for European options is best expressed as:
e: Put-call parity: C − P = S − X × e^(−r × t). Same strike, same expiry, European. Violation creates arbitrage opportunity.

q: An option with theta = −0.05 means the option will lose approximately:
e: Theta is expressed per unit (per share/per index point) per day. Theta = −0.05 means premium drops ₹0.05 per day, holding all else constant.

q: Implied volatility (IV) of an option is:
o: The historical volatility of the underlying
The volatility input that, in the pricing model, returns the observed market premium
e: IV is the volatility number that, plugged into the Black-Scholes (or other) pricing formula, makes the model price equal to the observed market premium. It reflects the market's collective view on future volatility.

q: Which option pricing model uses a discrete tree and can value American-style options?
e: The CRR binomial model uses a discrete time tree, accommodates dividends, and handles American options where early exercise is possible. Black-Scholes assumes European exercise.

q: The lot size for an index options contract is determined by:
e: Exchanges determine lot size, which is reviewed periodically to keep contract value within SEBI's prescribed band (₹15-20 lakh post Nov 2024).

q: A long call holder's maximum possible loss is:
e: Maximum loss for an option buyer is the premium paid — the option simply expires worthless if not exercised.

q: Closing a long call position is done by:
o: Buying a put on the same strike
e: An option position is closed by an offsetting trade with the SAME terms (strike + expiry). For a long call, that's a closing sale of the same call.

q: The 'assignment' of an option means:
o: The buyer transferring rights to another
Allocation of an exercised option to one or more option sellers
The exchange reassigning a clearing member
e: When the option holder exercises, the clearing corporation 'assigns' the obligation to one (or more) writers — usually proportional to outstanding short position.

q: Gamma is highest for options that are:
e: Gamma (rate of change of delta) is highest near the money and falls toward zero for deep ITM and deep OTM options. ATM options have the most curvature.

q: Final settlement of European-style index options happens at the:
o: Closing spot value of the underlying on expiry
e: European options settle at the closing spot value of the underlying on expiry — same reference as the corresponding futures contract.

q: If a call option's intrinsic value is ₹0 and premium is ₹15, the time value is:
e: Time value = Premium − Intrinsic value = 15 − 0 = ₹15. The entire premium is time value when the option is OTM or ATM.

q: Theta is positive for which of the following positions?
e: Theta is positive for short options (call or put) — the writer earns value as time decays. It is negative for long options (the buyer's premium erodes daily).
